estrogen deficiency is the predominant cause of the early, accelerated phase of bone loss, but it is not the only cause of the late slow phase of bone loss.
estrogen deficiency, while the predominant cause of bone loss, is not the only cause of bone loss in men and women.

the pathogenesis of postmenopausal osteoporosis in women and age‐related bone loss in men is a complex multifactorial process that involves multiple hormones and other factors that act in concert to regulate bone mass and structure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are not as far away from a cure for osteoporosis as we once thought, and we should not lose sight of that goal.
estrogen deficiency plays the predominant role in the pathogenesis of cortical bone loss but is less important for trabecular bone.
estrogen deficiency is a major determinant of bone loss in women, but it is not the only one.
The main takeaway from our work is that
estrogen deficiency is a major determinant of bone loss in humans and is likely to be the predominant driver of bone loss in women.
bone loss is not simply due to estrogen deficiency but rather that estrogen is one of many hormones and growth factors that contribute to bone loss, especially in the trabecular compartment.
bone is a tissue that is highly sensitive to the levels of estrogen, and that estrogen is the predominant driver for bone loss in post-menopausal women.
